kurals.tamil:
உறுப்பமைந்து ஊறஞ்சா வெல்படை வேந்தன்
வெறுக்கையுள் எல்லாம் தலை.
kurals.transliteration:
Uruppamaindhu ooranjaa velpadai vendhan
verukkaiyul ellaam thalai.
kurals.meaning: An army that is complete in all its parts and wins without fearing wounds is the foremost of all the treasures a king possesses.
kurals.elementary: Think of a school sports team where every position is filled, everyone has practised, and nobody is scared of a hard game. A coach would say that team is worth more than any trophy cupboard. Valluvar says a king’s well-prepared army is like that: his most precious possession.
kurals.university: The chapter opens the Padai-iyal (the section on the army), and its first couplet ranks the army above every other form of veṟukkai (வெறுக்கை, ‘wealth, treasure’). Uṟuppu (உறுப்பு, ‘limb’) is read by Parimelazhagar as the traditional four limbs of an Indian army, elephants, chariots, horse and foot, so uṟuppamaintu means ‘complete in its divisions’; ūṟu (ஊறு) is ‘wound’ or ‘harm’, and ūṟañcā ‘not dreading injury’. The logic echoes kural 381, which lists the army (படை) first among the six limbs of a kingdom, and the Arthashastra’s list of seven elements of sovereignty. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar gloss the line almost identically; Solomon Pappaiah modernizes the ‘limbs’ as land, sea and air forces and police. The ytamizh and thirukkural-thamizh texts agree, differing only in sandhi (உறுப்பமைந் தூறஞ்சா).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “THE king, the minister, the country, the fort, the treasury, the army and the friend are the elements of sovereignty.”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya lists the army as one of the seven constituent elements without which a state cannot stand, and then describes the qualities of the best army in detail.
hinduism.tie_back: Valluvar goes a step further, ranking a complete, fearless army first among a king’s treasures.
hinduism.source: Kautilya, Arthashastra, Book VI, Chapter 1 (trans. R. Shamasastry)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close in subject and genre; Kautilya lists the army among seven elements rather than ranking it highest.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Or what king, going to make war against another king, sitteth not down first, and consulteth whether he be able with ten thousand to meet him that cometh against him with twenty thousand?”
christianity.explanation: Jesus uses a king weighing the strength of his army as an image of counting the cost before committing to discipleship.
christianity.tie_back: The parable assumes what the Kural states: a king’s real security rests on the army he can actually field.
christianity._accuracy_note: The parable’s point is spiritual cost-counting; the military assessment is only its illustration.

islam.quote_or_event: “And prepare against them whatever you are able of power and of steeds of war by which you may terrify the enemy of Allah and your enemy and others besides them whom you do not know [but] whom Allah knows.”
islam.explanation: The community is told to keep its forces as fully equipped as it can, both cavalry and every other kind of strength.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats a fully equipped, ready force as a primary duty and asset of the polity.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match on preparedness and completeness; the Qur’an frames it as religious duty rather than royal wealth.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And Uzziah prepared for them, even for all the host, shields, and spears, and helmets, and coats of mail, and bows, and stones for slinging.”
judaism.explanation: The Chronicler presents Uzziah’s trained army of over three hundred thousand, fully equipped, as a mark of his strength while he sought God.
judaism.tie_back: A complete, well-armed host is pictured as a king’s chief strength, as in the Kural.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close on a fully equipped army as royal strength; the chapter later warns that the strength made Uzziah proud.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Excellent are well-trained mules, thoroughbred Sindhu horses and noble tusker elephants. But better still is the man who has subdued himself.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha grants that the trained animals of a royal army are excellent, then points to self-mastery as the higher prize.
buddhism.tie_back: It shares the Kural’s admiration for well-trained army ‘limbs’, while redirecting the idea of the greatest treasure inward.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Partial match; the verse uses army animals as a foil for self-discipline.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Herodotus describes Xerxes’ ten thousand Persian ‘Immortals’, a corps kept always at full strength: whenever a man dropped out, another was chosen to take his place.
greek_mythology.explanation: The elite unit’s prestige came from never being incomplete, and it was the pride of the Persian king’s host.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It illustrates the Kural’s uṟuppamaintu, an army complete in all its parts, as a king’s prized possession.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Historical rather than mythological, and paraphrased from memory of the passage rather than verified verbatim.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “These are: (1) The Moral Law; (2) Heaven; (3) Earth; (4) The Commander; (5) Method and discipline.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu lists the five constant factors by which a ruler should judge the strength of an army before going to war.
philosophy.tie_back: Like Valluvar, Sun Tzu treats a complete, well-ordered army as something to be assessed and valued with care.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War 1.4 (trans. Lionel Giles)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Shares the theme of a complete, well-ordered army but does not call it the king’s chief wealth.

kurals.tamil:
உலைவிடத்து ஊறஞ்சா வன்கண் தொலைவிடத்துத்
தொல்படைக் கல்லால் அரிது.
kurals.transliteration:
Ulaividaththu ooranjaa vankan tholaividaththuth
tholpadaik kallaal aridhu.
kurals.meaning: The courage to stand firm in defeat, unafraid of injury even when the ranks have thinned, is rarely found in anything but a long-established army.
kurals.elementary: When a team is losing badly, new players often give up, but players who have trained together for years keep going. They have been through hard games before. Valluvar says an old, experienced army is like that: it keeps its courage even when things are going wrong.
kurals.university: Ulaivu (உலைவு) means ‘reverse, setback’ and tolaivu (தொலைவு) ‘diminution, loss of numbers’, so the couplet describes valour (vaṉkaṇ, வன்கண்) that survives both defeat and attrition. Tolpaṭai (தொல்படை, ‘ancient army’) is read by Parimelazhagar as the hereditary core force (often called மூலப்படை in the commentarial tradition), as against hired or allied troops, a distinction that closely parallels Kautilya’s preference for hereditary troops. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar follow this reading, while Solomon Pappaiah extends tolpaṭai to native citizen-soldiers whose families have long lived in the land. The text is identical in both sources apart from sandhi (வன்கண் டொலைவிடத்துத் in the joined text).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Coming down directly, from father and grandfather (of the king), ever strong, obedient, happy in keeping their sons and wives well contented, not averse to making a long sojourn, ever and everywhere invincible, endowed with the power of endurance...”
hinduism.explanation: Kautilya’s description of the best army begins with its hereditary character and stresses endurance and steadiness.
hinduism.tie_back: This is almost exactly Valluvar’s tolpaṭai: a hereditary army whose endurance holds when fortunes turn.
hinduism.source: Kautilya, Arthashastra, Book VI, Chapter 1 (trans. R. Shamasastry)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on hereditary troops and endurance.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Thou therefore endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells Timothy that the mark of a good soldier is the capacity to endure hardship.
christianity.tie_back: Endurance under hardship is the very valour the Kural assigns to a seasoned army.
christianity._accuracy_note: Metaphorical soldiering; shares the endurance theme but not the point about long-established troops.

islam.quote_or_event: “And how many a prophet [fought and] with him fought many religious scholars. But they never lost assurance due to what afflicted them in the cause of Allah, nor did they weaken or submit. And Allah loves the steadfast.”
islam.explanation: Revealed after the setback at Uhud, the verse holds up earlier companions of prophets who did not weaken when they were struck by losses.
islam.tie_back: It praises the same courage the Kural describes: steadiness when the fight is going badly.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match on steadfastness in reverses; the hereditary element is absent.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Hear, O Israel, ye draw nigh this day unto battle against your enemies; let not your heart faint; fear not, nor be alarmed, neither be ye affrighted at them.”
judaism.explanation: Before battle the priest addresses the army, telling it not to lose heart even when the enemy seems stronger.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘fearless valour’ is exactly what this exhortation tries to instil in Israel’s host.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good match on courage; it is a pre-battle exhortation rather than praise of a veteran army in defeat.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “As an elephant in the battlefield withstands arrows shot from bows all around, even so shall I endure abuse.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares his patience to a trained war-elephant that holds its ground under a shower of arrows.
buddhism.tie_back: The image is the Kural’s ūṟañcā vaṉkaṇ, a seasoned fighter unshaken by wounds.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Vivid parallel on enduring blows; applied to patience under insult rather than to an army.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad, when the Trojans drive the Achaeans back to their ships, Ajax son of Telamon stays at the sterns and keeps fighting off the attackers long after others have given way.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ajax is the Iliad’s great picture of defensive steadiness when the battle has turned against his side.
greek_mythology.tie_back: He embodies the Kural’s courage in the hour of defeat.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; Ajax is a single hero rather than a long-established army.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Laches, the general Laches first defines courage as staying at one’s post and not running away, then refines it to a kind of endurance of the soul; Socrates presses that it must be wise endurance.
philosophy.explanation: The dialogue examines what military courage really is, rooted in steadfast endurance under danger.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar locates exactly this endurance in a veteran army facing defeat.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased summary; the dialogue is inconclusive about the final definition.

kurals.tamil:
ஒலித்தக்கால் என்னாம் உவரி எலிப்பகை
நாகம் உயிர்ப்பக் கெடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Oliththakkaal ennaam uvari elippakai
naagam uyirppak kedum.
kurals.meaning: What does it matter if a host of rats roars like the sea? At a single breath of the cobra they are scattered and ruined.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a crowd of mice squeaking very loudly in a barn. It sounds scary, but the moment a snake hisses, they all scurry away. Valluvar says a big, noisy army with no real courage is like those mice, and a small, brave army is like the snake.
kurals.university: The couplet is a celebrated uvamai (simile): uvari (உவரி, ‘the salt sea’) describes the roar of a vast but timid enemy, while nākam (நாகம், ‘cobra’) and uyirppa (உயிர்ப்ப, ‘as it breathes, hisses’) picture a small force of real valour. Parimelazhagar reads it as a statement that numbers without courage count for nothing against a brave army, and Solomon Pappaiah explicitly makes the cobra a small army and the rats a large one ‘rat-like in mind’. Kalaignar applies it to a single hero rising in anger. The text is the same in both sources apart from sandhi (ஒலித்தக்கா லென்னா முவரி யெலிப்பகை).

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Mahabharata, the Pandavas field seven akshauhinis against the Kauravas’ eleven, yet the larger host is defeated at Kurukshetra.
hinduism.explanation: The epic repeatedly stresses that the numerically superior Kaurava army lacked the righteousness and leadership that sustained the smaller force.
hinduism.tie_back: It is the Kural’s point on an epic scale: a great noisy host gives way before a smaller, stronger one.
hinduism.source: Mahabharata, Udyoga and Bhishma Parvas (trans. K. M. Ganguli)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Well-known narrative outline paraphrased; the outcome is long and complex rather than instant like the cobra’s hiss.

christianity.quote_or_event: When the king of Aram surrounds Dothan with horses and chariots, Elisha tells his frightened servant that those with them are more than those with the enemy, and his eyes are opened to see the hills full of horses and chariots of fire.
christianity.explanation: The story teaches that a vast visible host does not decide the outcome.
christianity.tie_back: Like the rats roaring like the sea, the besieging army looks overwhelming yet comes to nothing.
christianity._accuracy_note: Paraphrased, not verified verbatim; the victory is divine rather than due to the valour of a small army.

islam.quote_or_event: “How many a small company has overcome a large company by permission of Allah. And Allah is with the patient.”
islam.explanation: As Talut’s (Saul’s) small band faced Jalut (Goliath) and his soldiers, the believers among them affirmed that a small company can overcome a large one.
islam.tie_back: This is the cobra and the rats: size of host matters less than steadfast courage.
islam._accuracy_note: Very close thematic match; the Qur’an attributes victory to God’s permission.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Come and let us go over unto the garrison of these uncircumcised; it may be that the LORD will work for us; for there is no restraint to the LORD to save by many or by few.”
judaism.explanation: Jonathan and his armour-bearer alone climb up to a Philistine garrison, and the whole Philistine camp falls into panic and melts away.
judaism.tie_back: A tiny, fearless force scattering a large host is exactly the Kural’s cobra among the rats.
judaism._accuracy_note: Strong match; the text credits God’s help as well as Jonathan’s daring.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Padhana Sutta, Mara’s ‘army’ of desire, discontent, hunger, craving, sloth and fear gathers around the Bodhisatta, who declares that he will not be driven from his place and defeats it by insight.
buddhism.explanation: A vast and clamorous host is overcome by one steadfast mind.
buddhism.tie_back: It mirrors the Kural’s image: a roaring multitude is undone by a single, truly strong presence.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; the ‘army’ is a metaphor for mental defilements.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Herodotus tells how the Athenians at Marathon, heavily outnumbered, charged the Persian army at a run and put it to flight.
greek_mythology.explanation: The Persians thought the Athenians mad to attack so few against so many, yet the smaller, determined force prevailed.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is a historical instance of the Kural’s rats scattered at the cobra’s breath.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Historical rather than mythological; paraphrased from the narrative.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Xenophon, rallying the Greek officers after their generals were seized, tells them that it is neither numbers nor strength that wins battles, but that whichever side advances with stouter hearts, the enemy generally will not stand against it.
philosophy.explanation: Stranded deep in Persian territory, Xenophon argues that morale, not size, decides the issue.
philosophy.tie_back: Valluvar’s cobra and rats make the same claim about courage versus numbers.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close thematic match; paraphrased because the translation could not be verified verbatim online.

kurals.tamil:
அழிவின்றி அறைபோகா தாகி வழிவந்த
வன்க ணதுவே படை.
kurals.transliteration:
Azhivindri araipogaa thaagi vazhivandha
vankanadhuve padai.
kurals.meaning: That alone is an army which has not been destroyed, cannot be bought over by the enemy, and carries a courage handed down through generations.
kurals.elementary: Imagine a family that has played in the same village band for generations. Nobody could pay them to play for a rival band, and they never give up halfway through a parade. Valluvar says a true army is like that: loyal, steady, and brave because bravery runs in its history.
kurals.university: Three marks define the true army here: aḻiviṉmai (not being broken in battle), aṟaipōkāmai (அறைபோகாமை, not being undermined or won over by enemy intrigue, i.e. free of treachery and desertion), and vaḻivanta vaṉkaṇ (வழிவந்த வன்கண், valour inherited through lineage). Parimelazhagar takes aṟaipōtal as being corrupted by the enemy’s secret approaches, and Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as ‘not falling prey to the enemy’s deceit’. There is a small textual variant: ytamizh prints அழிவின்றி, while the sandhi-joined thirukkural-thamizh text reads அழிவின் றறைபோகா, i.e. அழிவின்று; the sense, ‘without destruction’, is unchanged.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “...ready to share in the weal or woe of the king, and consequently not falling foul with him...”
hinduism.explanation: In Kautilya’s description of the best army, hereditary troops are prized because they share the king’s fortunes and do not turn against him.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s aṟaipōkāmai and vaḻivanta vaṉkaṇ: loyalty and inherited valour.
hinduism.source: Kautilya, Arthashastra, Book VI, Chapter 1 (trans. R. Shamasastry)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Very close on hereditary, loyal troops.

christianity.quote_or_event: “No man that warreth entangleth himself with the affairs of this life; that he may please him who hath chosen him to be a soldier.”
christianity.explanation: Paul describes the good soldier as one whose loyalty to his commander is not divided by other interests.
christianity.tie_back: An army that cannot be drawn away by other inducements is what the Kural means by one that does not ‘go over’.
christianity._accuracy_note: Thematic match on undivided loyalty; spiritual metaphor, and the hereditary element is absent.

islam.quote_or_event: The Qur’an warns believers that when they meet the enemy in battle they must not turn their backs, except to manoeuvre or to rejoin their own company.
islam.explanation: Desertion in the face of the enemy is condemned as a grave fault.
islam.tie_back: It parallels the Kural’s demand that a true army never breaks or goes over to the enemy.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrased, not verified verbatim; covers the anti-desertion element but not inherited valour.

judaism.quote_or_event: When David flees Jerusalem during Absalom’s revolt, the foreigner Ittai the Gittite refuses to leave him, vowing that wherever the king is, in death or in life, there his servant will be.
judaism.explanation: Ittai and his men stay loyal to David at the lowest point of his reign, when many others had gone over to Absalom.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s aṟaipōkāmai, troops who will not be won over by the other side.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; strong on loyalty, though Ittai is a newcomer rather than hereditary.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “What have you heard, Ananda: do the Vajjis neither enact new decrees nor abolish existing ones, but proceed in accordance with their ancient constitutions?”
buddhism.explanation: When King Ajatasattu plans to attack the Vajjis, the Buddha says they cannot be overcome so long as they keep to their ancient ways and remain united.
buddhism.tie_back: Strength drawn from long-held tradition is the Kural’s vaḻivanta vaṉkaṇ, valour that comes down through lineage.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 16, Mahaparinibbana Sutta 1.4 (trans. Sister Vajira & Francis Story)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Concerns a republic’s civic traditions rather than an army’s inherited courage.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Demaratus tells Xerxes that the Spartans are free but have law as their master, and that law commands them never to flee from battle whatever the size of the enemy, but to stand in their ranks and conquer or die.
greek_mythology.explanation: Spartan steadfastness is presented as an inherited discipline rather than individual bravado.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It matches the Kural’s army whose courage is handed down and which never breaks.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Close match; paraphrased because the translation could not be loaded for verbatim checking.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Machiavelli argues that a principality without its own arms is never secure, and that mercenary and auxiliary troops are useless and dangerous because they have no loyalty but pay.
philosophy.explanation: He urges rulers to rely on armies composed of their own subjects.
philosophy.tie_back: It is the political-philosophical form of the Kural’s point that only a native, long-established army will not desert.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong match; paraphrased rather than quoted.

kurals.tamil:
கூற்றுடன்று மேல்வரினும் கூடி எதிர்நிற்கும்
ஆற்ற லதுவே படை.
kurals.transliteration:
Kootrudandru melvarinum koodi edhirnirkum
aatraladhuve padai.
kurals.meaning: That alone is an army which has the strength to stand together and face the foe even if Death himself should come against it in fury.
kurals.elementary: Picture a group of friends holding hands in a line during a strong wind on the beach. Alone, each might be pushed over, but together they stay standing. Valluvar says a real army stands together like that, even against the scariest danger.
kurals.university: Kūṟṟu (கூற்று) is Death personified, identified by commentators with Yama, and uṭaṉṟu (உடன்று) means ‘having become enraged’. The key word is kūṭi (கூடி, ‘together, united’): the excellence praised is collective resolve rather than individual heroism, and āṟṟal (ஆற்றல்) is the strength to hold. Parimelazhagar notes that even the god of death cannot be resisted by ordinary means, so the hyperbole stresses unity as the army’s defining power. The two sources agree apart from sandhi (கூடி யெதிர்நிற்கு / மாற்ற லதுவே).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Do thou fight for the sake of fighting, without considering happiness or distress, loss or gain, victory or defeat—and, by so doing, you shall never incur sin.”
hinduism.explanation: Krishna urges Arjuna to face the battle with equanimity, unmoved by fear of loss or even death.
hinduism.tie_back: It reflects the Kural’s resolve to stand firm even when Death advances.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Matches fearlessness before outcome, but addresses an individual and lacks the theme of unity.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Wherefore take unto you the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells the church, addressed collectively, to be equipped to hold its ground on the worst of days.
christianity.tie_back: ‘Having done all, to stand’ is the Kural’s collective resistance even against Death.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close on standing firm in the evil day; the battle is spiritual.

islam.quote_or_event: “Indeed, Allah loves those who fight in His cause in a row as though they are a [single] structure joined firmly.”
islam.explanation: The sura named ‘The Ranks’ praises fighters who hold together like a solid building.
islam.tie_back: The firmly joined structure is exactly the Kural’s kūṭi etirniṟkum, standing together against the onslaught.
islam._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match on united resistance.

judaism.quote_or_event: While rebuilding Jerusalem’s walls under threat, Nehemiah arms the builders, tells them not to fear but to remember the LORD, and orders that wherever the trumpet sounds they should rally together there.
judaism.explanation: The scattered workers become a single defensive body ready to meet any attack.
judaism.tie_back: It embodies the Kural’s united stand against a threatening enemy.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; good on unity, though the threat never becomes a pitched battle.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “What have you heard, Ananda: do the Vajjis assemble and disperse peacefully and attend to their affairs in concord?” ... “So long, Ananda, as this is the case, the growth of the Vajjis is to be expected, not their decline.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells Ajatasattu’s minister that the Vajjis cannot be conquered while they remain united.
buddhism.tie_back: Concord as the source of invincibility is the heart of the Kural’s kūṭi, ‘standing together’.
buddhism.source: Digha Nikaya 16, Mahaparinibbana Sutta 1.4 (trans. Sister Vajira & Francis Story)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong match on unity as strength; set in civic rather than battlefield context.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “Divide your men, Agamemnon, into their several tribes and clans, that clans and tribes may stand by and help one another.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Nestor advises Agamemnon to array the Achaeans so that kin stand beside kin and support each other.
greek_mythology.tie_back: His counsel aims at the same mutual support that lets the Kural’s army stand together against Death.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Good match on cohesion; it is tactical advice rather than a picture of facing death.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The Moral Law causes the people to be in complete accord with their ruler, so that they will follow him regardless of their lives, undismayed by any danger.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu names moral unity between ruler and people as the first factor in war.
philosophy.tie_back: Complete accord that holds ‘regardless of their lives’ is the Kural’s united stand even against Death.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War 1.5–6 (trans. Lionel Giles)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Very close on unity and fearlessness before death.

kurals.tamil:
மறமானம் மாண்ட வழிச்செலவு தேற்றம்
எனநான்கே ஏமம் படைக்கு.
kurals.transliteration:
Maramaanam maanda vazhichchelavu thetram
enanaange emam padaikku.
kurals.meaning: Valour, honour, following the noble path of those who went before, and being trusted: these four alone are an army’s safeguard.
kurals.elementary: A good scout troop needs four things: brave members, members who care about doing the right thing, members who follow the good habits of older scouts, and a leader who can trust them. Valluvar says an army needs the same four things to stay safe and strong.
kurals.university: The couplet names four qualities: maṟam (மறம், valour), māṉam (மானம், honour, sense of shame at disgrace), māṇṭa vaḻiccelavu (மாண்ட வழிச்செலவு, walking the excellent path of predecessors), and tēṟṟam (தேற்றம்). Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar take tēṟṟam as ‘being trusted (tested and found reliable) by the king’, while Sivayogi Sivakumar renders it as ‘clear resolve’, a genuine interpretive divergence. Ēmam (ஏமம்) means ‘protection, safeguard’, and the emphatic nāṉkē (‘these four alone’) makes the list exclusive. Both sources agree on the wording (சந்தி: தேற்ற / மெனநான்கே யேமம்).

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna lists the natural qualities of the kshatriya, the warrior class, as heroism, power, determination, resourcefulness, courage in battle, generosity and leadership.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita defines the warrior by a set of inner virtues rather than by weapons.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s four safeguards, it sees a fighting force’s strength in valour, honour and character.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; overlaps on valour but the list differs from the Kural’s four.

christianity.quote_or_event: Paul describes the Christian’s armour as the belt of truth, the breastplate of righteousness, the readiness of the gospel of peace, the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit.
christianity.explanation: Each piece of protective equipment is matched to an inner virtue.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says a soldier’s real safeguard lies in qualities of character.
christianity._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; spiritual armour, and the virtues listed differ from the Kural’s four.

islam.quote_or_event: “And obey Allah and His Messenger, and do not dispute and [thus] lose courage and [then] your strength would depart; and be patient. Indeed, Allah is with the patient.”
islam.explanation: Before battle, believers are told that obedience, unity and patience preserve their courage and strength.
islam.tie_back: It names safeguards of an army, as the Kural does with its four, including trustworthy obedience.
islam._accuracy_note: Good match on qualities that protect an army; the list is not the same.

judaism.quote_or_event: “What man is there that is fearful and faint-hearted? let him go and return unto his house, lest his brethren’s heart melt as his heart.”
judaism.explanation: Torah law sends the faint-hearted home before battle so that fear does not spread through the ranks.
judaism.tie_back: Keeping only the valiant protects the army, echoing the Kural’s maṟam as its first safeguard.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha says a king’s elephant is fit for royal service when it has four qualities: it listens, it destroys, it endures, and it goes quickly; a monk with the corresponding four qualities is worthy of offerings.
buddhism.explanation: The sutta uses a fourfold standard for a war-elephant as a model of spiritual fitness.
buddhism.tie_back: It parallels the Kural’s fourfold list of what makes an army trustworthy and secure.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from memory of the sutta, not verified verbatim; the four qualities differ.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Plutarch records the Spartan mother who handed her son his shield with the words ‘either this or upon this’, meaning return with it or be carried home on it.
greek_mythology.explanation: The saying captures Spartan honour: to lose one’s shield in flight was the deepest disgrace.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It embodies the Kural’s māṉam, honour, as a safeguard of the army.
greek_mythology.source: Plutarch, Moralia, Sayings of Spartan Women 241F
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased anecdote; it covers honour only, one of the four.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The Commander stands for the virtues of wisdom, sincerity, benevolence, courage and strictness.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu defines military excellence in terms of a short list of moral virtues.
philosophy.tie_back: Like Valluvar, he names a compact set of character qualities as the army’s real protection.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War 1.9 (trans. Lionel Giles)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Close in form (a list of virtues), but applied to the commander and not identical in content.

kurals.tamil:
தார்தாங்கிச் செல்வது தானை தலைவந்த
போர்தாங்கும் தன்மை அறிந்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Thaarthaangich chelvadhu thaanai thalaivandha
poarthaangum thanmai arindhu.
kurals.meaning: A true army knows how to withstand the attack that comes upon it, and so advances bearing the brunt of the enemy’s vanguard.
kurals.elementary: In a game of tug-of-war, the strongest kids stand at the front where the pull is hardest, and they know how to dig their heels in. Valluvar says a good army is like that: it knows how to take the first hard push and keep moving forward.
kurals.university: Tār (தார்) is the vanguard, called tūci (தூசி) in the commentaries, which Pope rendered ‘dust-van’ after the dust raised by an advancing force; tāṉai (தானை) is the army. Parimelazhagar reads the couplet as describing an army that, knowing the art of checking an oncoming assault (talaivanta pōr tāṅkum taṉmai), meets and bears the enemy’s vanguard. Solomon Pappaiah reads tār more broadly as the front-line foot soldiers, while Sivayogi Sivakumar takes it as an image of ranks arrayed like a banana bunch, an idiosyncratic reading. Both texts agree (சந்தி: போர்தாங்குந் தன்மை யறிந்து).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Now all of you must give full support to Grandfather Bhīṣma, standing at your respective strategic points in the phalanx of the army.”
hinduism.explanation: Duryodhana orders his commanders to hold their positions in the formation so that the line is not broken.
hinduism.tie_back: Holding one’s place in the array to meet the oncoming assault is what the Kural asks of a true army.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Matches the idea of holding formation; spoken by a flawed leader and not about the vanguard specifically.

christianity.quote_or_event: The apostle Peter urges believers to be watchful because the adversary prowls like a lion, and to resist him steadfast in the faith.
christianity.explanation: The faithful are told to stand their ground against an attack rather than give way.
christianity.tie_back: Meeting the oncoming assault and withstanding it is the Kural’s description of a true army.
christianity._accuracy_note: Paraphrased and metaphorical; weak on the military-formation sense.

islam.quote_or_event: At Uhud the Prophet stationed a company of archers on a hill and ordered them not to leave their post; when most of them left it, the Muslim line was turned, and the Qur’an refers to this disobedience and dispute.
islam.explanation: The episode shows that the outcome depended on holding the assigned position against the enemy’s charge.
islam.tie_back: It illustrates by contrast the Kural’s army that knows how to bear the enemy’s attack.
islam.source: Qur’an 3:152 and the sira accounts of Uhud
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a negative example, and the Qur’anic verse alludes to rather than narrates the event.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And they stood every man in his place round about the camp; and all the host ran; and they shouted, and fled.”
judaism.explanation: Gideon’s three hundred hold their positions around the Midianite camp, and the vast host breaks and flees.
judaism.tie_back: Each man holding his place as the enemy surges is the Kural’s army that bears the assault and advances.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good match on holding position; the enemy flees rather than charges.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “There is the case of a warrior who, on seeing a cloud of dust [stirred up by the enemy army], falters, faints, doesn’t steel himself, can’t engage in the battle.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha ranks warriors by how far they can withstand the stages of an enemy advance, from the dust cloud to hand-to-hand combat.
buddhism.tie_back: The best warrior who bears the ‘cloud of dust’ is exactly the Kural’s army that bears the dust-van of the foe.
buddhism.source: Anguttara Nikaya 5.75, Yodhajiva Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Striking parallel on withstanding the vanguard; the sutta’s application is to monastic discipline.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad, Nestor arrays the Pylians with charioteers in front, a mass of brave foot soldiers behind as a bulwark, and the less reliable men placed in the middle so that they must fight.
greek_mythology.explanation: The wise old king shows how an army’s arrangement lets it absorb and repel an attack.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Knowing how to bear the oncoming assault through good order is the Kural’s point.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from the passage, not verified verbatim.

philosophy.quote_or_event: During the retreat of the Ten Thousand, the Greeks formed a hollow square with baggage in the centre and reorganised their rearguard so that they could keep marching while bearing the Persians’ harassing attacks.
philosophy.explanation: Xenophon describes the practical skill of an army that advances while absorbing pressure.
philosophy.tie_back: It is the Kural’s army that ‘knows how to bear the attack’ and keeps going.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; the pressure comes at the rear and flanks rather than from a vanguard.

kurals.tamil:
அடல்தகையும் ஆற்றலும் இல்லெனினும் தானை
படைத்தகையால் பாடு பெறும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Adalthagaiyum aatralum illeninum thaanai
padaiththagaiyaal paadu perum.
kurals.meaning: Even if it lacks the power to attack and the strength to resist, an army can win renown by the splendour of its array and equipment.
kurals.elementary: A marching band in smart uniforms, all in step, can make a whole crowd stop and stare, even before it plays a note. Valluvar says an army that is neatly lined up and well equipped can earn respect just by how it looks and moves.
kurals.university: Aṭaltakai (அடல்தகை) is the capacity to attack and destroy, āṟṟal (ஆற்றல்) the capacity to withstand; paṭaittakai (படைத்தகை) is the excellence of the army’s equipment and array, and pāṭu (பாடு) means ‘renown, dignity’. Parimelazhagar understands the couplet as saying that order and splendour alone can deter or impress an enemy, and Solomon Pappaiah stresses the disciplined beauty of its formation. Kalaignar reads it slightly differently, as saying the array should be even more excellent than attack and defence. The two sources agree (சந்தி: அடல்தகையு மாற்றலு மில்லெனினுந் தானை).

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya devotes Book X of the Arthashastra to the arraying of troops (vyuha), naming formations such as the staff, the snake, the circle and the detached array, and how each is to be ordered for battle.
hinduism.explanation: The treatise treats the correct array of an army as a science in itself.
hinduism.tie_back: It shares the Kural’s conviction that an army’s formation and order are a source of strength and prestige.
hinduism.source: Kautilya, Arthashastra, Book X, Chapters 5–6 (trans. R. Shamasastry)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased summary; Kautilya treats array as tactics rather than as a source of renown.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Or else, while the other is yet a great way off, he sendeth an ambassage, and desireth conditions of peace.”
christianity.explanation: In Jesus’ parable, the weaker king, seeing the size of the advancing army, sues for peace before any battle.
christianity.tie_back: An army can win its ends by its mere appearance and strength, as the Kural says.
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches the deterrent effect; the parable’s purpose is spiritual cost-counting.

islam.quote_or_event: Before the conquest of Mecca, the Muslim army lit many campfires and paraded past Abu Sufyan, whose sight of its numbers and order contributed to the city’s surrender largely without fighting.
islam.explanation: The display of a well-ordered force secured the result that battle might otherwise have decided.
islam.tie_back: It illustrates the Kural’s claim that an army can win distinction by its array alone.
islam.source: Sira accounts of the conquest of Mecca (Ibn Ishaq)
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrased from the traditional narrative; the army did not lack fighting strength.

judaism.quote_or_event: “And he made in Jerusalem engines, invented by skilful men, to be on the towers and upon the corners, wherewith to shoot arrows and great stones. And his name spread far abroad; for he was marvellously helped, till he was strong.”
judaism.explanation: Uzziah’s equipment and engines spread his fame far beyond Judah.
judaism.tie_back: Renown earned through the excellence of an army’s equipment is the Kural’s paṭaittakaiyāl pāṭu.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close on fame through equipment; the next verses warn that it led to pride.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “A tamed elephant is led into a crowd, and the king mounts a tamed elephant. Best among men is the subdued one who endures abuse.”
buddhism.explanation: The trained elephant is the one fit to be shown before crowds and to carry the king.
buddhism.tie_back: Discipline that earns public honour parallels the Kural’s army renowned for its order.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Partial match; the point is self-discipline, with the war-elephant as illustration.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Herodotus describes Xerxes reviewing his vast army at Doriscus, riding past nation after nation in their distinctive arms and dress, an array famed throughout Greece.
greek_mythology.explanation: The splendour of the Persian host was itself a weapon, meant to awe the Greeks into submission.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It shows the renown an army can gain by its array alone, though the campaign later failed.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; also a cautionary example, since splendour did not bring victory.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Hence to fight and conquer in all your battles is not supreme excellence; supreme excellence consists in breaking the enemy’s resistance without fighting.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu prizes winning through position and strength over actual combat.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s army that wins distinction by its array without fighting is a case of this ideal.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War 3.2 (trans. Lionel Giles)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Good fit on winning without battle; Sun Tzu stresses strategy more than outward display.

kurals.tamil:
சிறுமையும் செல்லாத் துனியும் வறுமையும்
இல்லாயின் வெல்லும் படை.
kurals.transliteration:
Sirumaiyum sellaath thuniyum varumaiyum
illaayin vellum padai.
kurals.meaning: An army will win if it is free from dwindling numbers, from lasting discontent, and from want.
kurals.elementary: A team does best when nobody keeps quitting, nobody is sulking and angry at the coach, and everyone has enough food and kit. Valluvar says an army is the same: keep it whole, happy and well supplied, and it will win.
kurals.university: Three defects are named: ciṟumai (சிறுமை, diminution, a shrinking of numbers or strength), cellāt tuṉi (செல்லாத் துனி, a resentment that will not go away, which Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar direct specifically against the king or commander), and vaṟumai (வறுமை, poverty, i.e. unpaid or ill-supplied troops). Solomon Pappaiah follows this reading, while Sivayogi Sivakumar renders ciṟumai as ‘confusion’, a looser gloss. The couplet’s realism about morale and pay matches Kautilya’s detailed discussion of an army’s ‘calamities’. Both sources agree (சந்தி: சிறுமையுஞ் ... வறுமையு / மில்லாயின்).

hinduism.quote_or_event: Kautilya discusses the ‘calamities of the army’, among them troops that are unpaid, disaffected, reduced in numbers, or harbouring grievances against the king, and weighs which are hardest to remedy.
hinduism.explanation: The treatise treats pay, morale and strength as conditions without which an army cannot fight well.
hinduism.tie_back: These are the very three defects, dwindling, discontent and want, that the Kural says an army must be free of.
hinduism.source: Kautilya, Arthashastra, Book VIII, Chapter 5 (trans. R. Shamasastry)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Close in content; paraphrased because the chapter was not loaded for verbatim checking.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Every kingdom divided against itself is brought to desolation; and every city or house divided against itself shall not stand.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus answers his critics with a proverb about internal division leading to ruin.
christianity.tie_back: An army eaten by lasting resentment, as the Kural warns, is a house divided against itself.

islam.quote_or_event: “So if there are from you one hundred [who are] steadfast, they will overcome two hundred. And if there are among you a thousand, they will overcome two thousand by permission of Allah. And Allah is with the steadfast.”
islam.explanation: The verse acknowledges weakness among the believers and sets a realistic ratio for a steadfast force.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it links victory to the inner condition of the troops rather than to numbers alone.
islam._accuracy_note: Partial match on morale and strength; it does not address pay or grievance.

judaism.quote_or_event: “My father hath troubled the land; see, I pray you, how mine eyes are brightened, because I tasted a little of this honey. How much more, if haply the people had eaten freely to-day of the spoil of their enemies which they found? had there not been then a much greater slaughter among the Philistines?”
judaism.explanation: Jonathan argues that Saul’s oath forbidding food left the troops faint and blunted their victory.
judaism.tie_back: It shows the Kural’s point that an army in want cannot win as it should.
judaism._accuracy_note: Good match on the ‘want’ element; the hunger is self-imposed by the king’s oath.

buddhism.quote_or_event: At Kosambi the monks fell into a bitter quarrel that would not be settled; the Buddha urged reconciliation, and when they would not listen he withdrew to dwell alone.
buddhism.explanation: The episode shows how a community paralysed by lasting resentment loses its strength and purpose.
buddhism.tie_back: It is a monastic picture of the Kural’s cellāt tuṉi, the grievance that will not go away.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased; a monastic community rather than an army.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Iliad, Achilles, aggrieved at Agamemnon for taking his prize, withdraws himself and his Myrmidons from the fighting, and the Achaeans suffer heavy reverses until the quarrel is resolved.
greek_mythology.explanation: The epic is built on the cost of an unresolved grievance between a leader and his best warriors.
greek_mythology.tie_back: It is the classic illustration of the Kural’s cellāt tuṉi, lasting discontent with the commander.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Strong match on grievance against the leader; paraphrased.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “By Method and discipline are to be understood the marshalling of the army in its proper subdivisions, the gradations of rank among the officers, the maintenance of roads by which supplies may reach the army, and the control of military expenditure.”
philosophy.explanation: Sun Tzu counts supply lines and the control of military spending among the basic factors of war.
philosophy.tie_back: Keeping an army supplied and paid answers the Kural’s warning against vaṟumai.
philosophy.source: Sun Tzu, The Art of War 1.10 (trans. Lionel Giles)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Matches the supply element; does not address grievance or dwindling numbers.

kurals.tamil:
நிலைமக்கள் சால உடைத்தெனினும் தானை
தலைமக்கள் இல்வழி இல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Nilaimakkal saala udaiththeninum thaanai
thalaimakkal ilvazhi il.
kurals.meaning: Though an army has a great many steadfast soldiers, it cannot stand where there are no worthy leaders.
kurals.elementary: A choir may have lots of good singers, but without a conductor they start and stop at different times and it sounds like a mess. Valluvar says an army is the same: many brave soldiers are not enough without a good leader.
kurals.university: Nilaimakkaḷ (நிலைமக்கள்) are ‘steadfast men’, read by Parimelazhagar as long-serving, permanent soldiers, and cāla (சால) means ‘in abundance’; talaimakkaḷ (தலைமக்கள்) are the ‘head-men’, i.e. commanders or generals. The final il vaḻi il (இல்வழி இல்) is a terse play: ‘where they are not, (the army) is not’, which Mu. Varadarasanar glosses as the army having no glory and Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar as its not being able to hold its ground. The couplet closes the chapter by turning from the troops to their leadership, preparing for the next chapter, Paṭaiccerukku (படைச்செருக்கு, the martial pride of warriors). Both sources agree (சந்தி: சால வுடைத்தெனினுந் ... தலைமக்க ளில்வழி யில்).

hinduism.quote_or_event: “Our strength is immeasurable, and we are perfectly protected by Grandfather Bhīṣma, whereas the strength of the Pāṇḍavas, carefully protected by Bhīma, is limited.”
hinduism.explanation: Duryodhana measures the two armies chiefly by the generals who lead and protect them.
hinduism.tie_back: His reasoning assumes the Kural’s point: an army’s worth depends on its commander.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Shares the premise that leaders define an army’s strength; spoken by a misjudging king, and other translations render the verse differently.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For if the trumpet give an uncertain sound, who shall prepare himself to the battle?”
christianity.explanation: Paul uses the image of an unclear battle signal to argue for clear, intelligible speech in the church.
christianity.tie_back: Without a clear lead, as the Kural says, even willing soldiers cannot act as an army.
christianity._accuracy_note: Apt image of failed leadership; Paul’s subject is speaking in tongues.

islam.quote_or_event: “O you who have believed, obey Allah and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you.”
islam.explanation: The community is commanded to follow rightful authority so that it acts as one body.
islam.tie_back: It assumes, like the Kural, that a body of people needs recognised leaders to be effective.
islam._accuracy_note: General principle of authority, not specific to armies.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Let the LORD, the God of the spirits of all flesh, set a man over the congregation, who may go out before them, and who may come in before them, and who may lead them out, and who may bring them in; that the congregation of the LORD be not as sheep which have no shepherd.”
judaism.explanation: Moses, nearing his death, asks God to appoint a leader for Israel, and Joshua is commissioned.
judaism.tie_back: ‘Go out before them’ is military language: without such a head, as the Kural says, the host is no host.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close on the necessity of a leader for a people about to go to war.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “If, dear sirs, when the devas have gone into battle, there should arise fear, terror, or horripilation, then on that occasion you should catch sight of the top of my standard. For when you have caught sight of the top of my standard, whatever fear, terror, or horripilation there is will be abandoned.”
buddhism.explanation: Sakka tells the gods’ army that the sight of their leader’s banner will steady them; the Buddha then offers the Triple Gem as a surer refuge.
buddhism.tie_back: An army steadied by sight of its leader is the Kural’s talaimakkaḷ principle.
buddhism.source: Samyutta Nikaya 11.3, Dhajagga Sutta (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong match on the leader’s role in an army’s courage; the sutta ultimately points beyond worldly leaders.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: “...we cannot all be kings; it is not well that there should be many masters; one man must be supreme—one king to whom the son of scheming Saturn has given the sceptre of sovereignty over you all.”
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus rallies the Achaeans, who are rushing for the ships, by insisting that an army needs one recognised leader.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The scene shows a host on the point of dissolving for want of command, as the Kural warns.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Close match on the need for leadership; Odysseus stresses unity of command.

philosophy.quote_or_event: After the Greek generals are seized, Xenophon tells the remaining officers that without commanders nothing fine or useful can be done anywhere, least of all in war, where good order saves men and disorder has already destroyed many; they elect new generals at once.
philosophy.explanation: The leaderless Ten Thousand recover only by choosing new commanders.
philosophy.tie_back: It is a direct historical demonstration of the Kural: many good soldiers, but no army, until leaders are found.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match; paraphrased because the translation could not be verified verbatim online.
